assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators opened a new classification of quantum matter: the quantum spin Hall state and three-dimensional topological insulators with protected surface states. The idea is conceptually deep, experimentally realised and has spread through condensed matter, photonics and quantum materials.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical core is Kane and Mele (with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposing HgTe, who are not on the supplied list). Molenkamp led the HgTe quantum spin Hall observation and Hasan the first 3D topological insulator observations (Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3). Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan form a theory plus two experiments configuration, but Mele and the HgTe proposers are left out, which is a real fairness problem.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation has been abundant and independent for about two decades, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether Mele, and the missing HgTe proposers, can be excluded fairly under the three-person limit.
Priority disputes over the first 3D topological insulator observation are not settled by the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable two-dimensional platform, and started the field of twistronics and moire quantum matter. The discovery is original and has strong lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulating and superconducting states and showed twist control. This is a clean theory plus experiment split. Experimental contributions from other groups (for example Dean, Young and Yazdani on related platforms) may be argued but are not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups since 2018. Understanding of the superconducting mechanism is still open, but the discovery itself is robust. Somewhat young, yet it is already a major field.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity and the correct treatment of correlations remain debated.
Allocation among experimental groups beyond the supplied names is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics realised strong light-matter coupling on a chip and underlies superconducting quantum processors and quantum-limited readout. It is a foundational technique with large impact on quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf proposed the architecture (2004); Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling. The three-person trio is plausible, but Girvin is omitted from the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature, widely reproduced and used in many platforms. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is adjacent, so the committee must judge how much new content this carries.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recently recognised superconducting-circuit prize and the omission of Girvin from the credit.
Whether this is judged a fundamental discovery or an enabling technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised controllable quantum many-body systems, from the superfluid to Mott insulator transition to quantum gas microscopy, and gave a means of simulating Hubbard-type models.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and collaborators proposed the Hubbard realisation with cold atoms; Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition (with Hansch's group), and Bloch built much of the later programme. Cirac is credited for simulation proposals, but I judge Bloch, Greiner and Zoller as the cleaner trio. Others, such as Jaksch and Hansch, are outside the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are well confirmed. The long-term scientific payoff (hard problems solved by quantum simulation) is still developing, so the case rests on the established lattice physics.
uncertainties: Whether the simulation claim is judged to have matured scientifically beyond the established Mott transition.
Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 AMO prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Baryon acoustic oscillations give a standard ruler from the early universe and a clean probe of dark energy and cosmic expansion. They link directly to the fundamental physics of the primordial plasma and give strong constraints on cosmological models.
assessment.attribution: Eisenstein and collaborators (SDSS LRG detection) and the 2dFGRS team (Cole, Peacock) reported the detection in 2005. Large collaboration work makes credit hard and the supplied names may not capture all decisive contributors (for example the original theory by Peebles, Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich, who are not listed).
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent surveys and now central to precision cosmology, including recent DESI results. Timely, although the 2011 prize already recognised accelerating expansion.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration credit and the theoretical priority of the standard-ruler idea.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Inflation addresses the horizon and flatness problems and explains the origin of primordial fluctuations; its predictions of near scale-invariant adiabatic perturbations match the cosmic microwave background in detail. It is among the most influential ideas in cosmology.
assessment.attribution: Guth, Linde, Starobinsky and others (Albrecht and Steinhardt, Sato) contributed the framework, while Mukhanov and Chibisov computed the perturbation spectrum. Starobinsky, Albrecht and Steinhardt are omitted, and the credit set is contested. A fair trio is hard to define.
assessment.maturity: The generic predictions are supported, but no direct evidence (for example primordial gravitational waves) isolates inflation from alternatives. This is the main reason to be cautious about timing.
uncertainties: Absence of direct evidence for primordial tensor modes.
Contested priority and difficulty selecting at most three people.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Gauge/gravity duality is a conceptually transformative result linking quantum gravity to field theory, with wide use in quantum field theory, black-hole physics and strongly coupled matter. I note, with my own background, that a Nobel Prize needs a discovery about nature.
assessment.attribution: Maldacena conjectured the duality; Gubser, Klebanov, Polyakov and Witten gave the precise dictionary. Polyakov, Witten and Maldacena form a natural trio, though Gubser and Klebanov are left out.
assessment.maturity: Mathematically extensively tested, but there is no direct empirical confirmation in nature, and applications to QCD plasma and condensed matter are only approximate. The prize criteria make this premature in my judgment.
uncertainties: No direct experimental test of the duality as a statement about our universe.
Whether the Nobel criterion of a discovery is satisfied by a theoretical conjecture.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Event Horizon Telescope produced the first images of black-hole shadows (M87* and Sgr A*), a direct test of strong-field gravity and accretion physics on horizon scales.
assessment.attribution: The result is a large collaboration product. Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the VLBI development and the collaboration, and Moran contributed to the early mm-VLBI work. Any trio omits many essential contributors, which is a serious difficulty for a fair prize.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by two sources and consistent with general relativity, but the images are still being refined, and the black-hole physics prizes of 2017, 2020 and others partly overlap. Recognition is somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Collaboration credit cannot be reduced fairly to three people.
Limited independent replication, since a single collaboration produced the images.
